The post Maya Higa built a wildlife sanctuary on Twitch, funded by the people who watch it first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
This article is part of The Optimist Daily’s Local Changemakers 2026 series, spotlighting changemakers 30 and under.

Image alt text: Maya Higa at Alveus Sanctuary with an animal ambassador during a live Twitch conservation education stream

Earlier this year, on a trip to Dominica to learn about the sperm whales that live in those Caribbean waters, Maya Higa was offered the chance to swim with them. She said no.

Her reason was simple. “She would not participate in an activity that her followers would not be able to do,” wrote Maggie Kaplan, who nominated Maya for this series and was on the same trip. For most wildlife creators, that would have been the perfect moment for the cameras to come out. Maya turned on her livestream instead, talked with the boat crew and local staff about their work and lives, and shared the whales from her view on the surface.

Kaplan came away moved by Maya’s resolve. “I was very impressed with her dedication on all fronts,” she wrote. But what she was describing wasn’t a sacrifice. It was consistency. Maya was doing exactly what she built Alveus Sanctuary to do.

Building Alveus

Maya founded Alveus in 2021 with a 21-hour charity stream on Twitch that raised more than $500,000. The platform came after the expertise, not the other way around.

She grew up in Northern California and studied agricultural education and communication at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo. In college, she took a job as a zookeeper and completed internships at AZA-accredited facilities. She even got her falconry license. Part of the work involved going to schools and birthday parties to teach kids about animals in person, which gave her a taste for hands-on outreach and education. She went on to become a licensed wildlife rehabilitator. When she started streaming, all of that prior knowledge and experience came with her.

Alveus is both a physical wildlife sanctuary in Austin, Texas, and a virtual education center. The sanctuary houses non-releasable animal ambassadors, animals that can’t survive in the wild but can represent their species and the ecosystems they come from. A 24/7 livestream on Twitch lets viewers watch them, get to know them by name, and connect with information about their wild counterparts. Other content creators can visit the sanctuary, run education programs, and extend the conservation message into communities Alveus wouldn’t otherwise reach.

What exactly is Alveus?

Alveus is both a physical wildlife sanctuary in Austin, Texas, and a virtual education center. The sanctuary houses non-releasable animal ambassadors, which are animals that can’t survive in the wild but can represent their species and the ecosystems they come from. A 24/7 livestream on Twitch lets viewers watch them, get to know them by name, and connect with information about their wild counterparts. Other content creators can visit the sanctuary, run education programs, and extend the conservation message into communities Alveus wouldn’t otherwise reach.

Conservation for a generation that grew up on Twitch

The demographic Maya is reaching is one that traditional conservation organizations have struggled with for years. Maya “is reaching a whole new generation of 18 to 30 year olds through social media platforms that speak to their demographic,” Kaplan wrote. That generation didn’t grow up watching nature documentaries on television. They watch streams, follow creators, and decide what they care about based on communities they already belong to.

“She is creating a new type of outreach,” Kaplan wrote, “a teaching platform about different species and their importance to our environment.” A teaching platform built around the creator-viewer relationship works differently from a broadcast. Viewers are compelled to come back. They recognize the individual animals. They get into discussions in the chat about things they’ve learned. Conservation education needs that kind of sustained attention, and with conventional methods, it doesn’t get it very often.

Maya has over a million followers across her platforms, and those followers have made Alveus financially self-sustaining through their donations. Twitch donated $100,000 to the sanctuary directly. A partnership with WWF extended the work beyond the sanctuary itself. And Maya’s own TED talk, “The wildlife sanctuary you can visit from anywhere,”that she delivered in London earlier this year brought the model to an even broader professional audience.

What comes next

By 2026, Alveus has raised more than $7.5 million for conservation causes since its founding. The organization is actively expanding: new animal ambassadors coming in, enclosures being built out, and staff added to keep pace.

Two projects are currently underway. The Pollinator Census is Alveus’s first community science initiative, where community members observe pollinator species in the sanctuary’s garden and entomologists identify them, generating data to support insect conservation research. The larger effort is the Alveus Research and Recovery Institute (ARRI), developed in partnership with the Association of Zoos and Aquariums‘ Saving Animals from Extinction (SAFE) program. ARRI’s first goal is a conservation breeding and release program for two critically endangered species: the Mexican Gray wolf and the Red wolf. It moves Alveus from education into direct intervention in species survival.

The sperm whale moment in Dominica illustrates something about the whole operation. Maya went to Dominica to learn. When the choice came up, she ran the same calculation she’s always run: the point isn’t the experience she gets to have. It’s the one her audience gets to share with her. With a million people watching, that adds up to a different kind of reach than the field has seen.

Learn more at bio.link/mayahiga.

articles.title: A 50-year-old mystery of vanishing frogs reveals a hidden killer
articles.summary: A nearly 50-year-old mystery involving disappearing frogs in Brazil may finally be solved, with scientists uncovering evidence that a deadly fungus swept through the region and devastated vulnerable species. Remarkably, many frog populations have since rebounded, suggesting they developed greater tolerance to the disease that once threatened their survival.
articles.content:
For nearly 50 years, scientists have struggled to explain why frogs began disappearing from Brazil's Atlantic Forest, one of the world's richest regions for amphibian diversity. Beginning in the 1970s, researchers documented dramatic population declines, but the cause of these losses remained uncertain.

Now, scientists have uncovered compelling evidence pointing to a deadly fungal disease as the likely explanation. The findings, published in Molecular Ecology, come from researchers at the Center for Conservation Genomics at the Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute (NZCBI) and Pennsylvania State University (PSU).

The suspected culprit is chytridiomycosis, often called chytrid, a disease caused by the microscopic fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis. Scientists believe the pathogen originated in Asia before spreading around the world during the 1970s and 1980s. However, the fungus was not formally identified and described until 1999, long after devastating amphibian declines had begun.

By then, hundreds of amphibian species worldwide had been driven toward extinction, and some had already disappeared. Because so many populations collapsed before scientists knew the fungus existed, determining whether it was responsible has been particularly difficult.

"After almost 50 years, we still aren't confident what caused many historical amphibian die-offs, making these declines some of the most enduring cold cases in wildlife epidemiology," said Jack Boyette, an NZCBI graduate fellow and doctoral candidate at PSU who led the research.

A 50-Year-Old Mystery in Brazil's Atlantic Forest

One of these longstanding mysteries centers on the Boracéia Biological Station in Brazil's Atlantic Forest, where amphibian populations experienced severe declines between 1979 and 1982.

Some researchers previously suggested that climate change or unusually extreme weather might have triggered the disappearances. The new findings, however, provide evidence that an emerging fungal disease was spreading through the area at precisely the same time.

"While environmental factors could have played a role, our findings most directly implicate the chytrid fungus, revealing that regional invasion of the pathogen coincided with these unexplained amphibian disappearances," Boyette said.

To investigate what happened, the researchers turned to an unexpected source of evidence: frogs preserved in museum collections decades earlier.

The Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History houses specimens collected by William Ronald Heyer, a former curator of amphibians and reptiles. Heyer conducted five collecting expeditions at Boracéia, including two during the 1970s before the major population declines and three during the 1980s after the die-offs had occurred.

These preserved animals offered scientists a rare opportunity to examine the period before and after the mysterious disappearances. By testing specimens collected at different times, researchers could investigate when the pathogen arrived and how rapidly it spread.

The team analyzed samples from more than 370 preserved amphibians representing 17 species, searching for evidence of chytrid infection and tracking how frequently the fungus appeared over time.

Museum Specimens Reveal a Deadly Fungal Outbreak

The results revealed a striking change. None of the specimens collected before 1979 showed evidence of chytrid infection. Among those collected during the 1980s, however, more than half tested positive for the fungus.

This sharp increase suggests that the pathogen arrived and spread through the local amphibian community around the same time that frog populations were collapsing.

But the researchers also uncovered a surprising pattern.

Species that suffered the most severe declines showed no detectable signs of infection in the preserved specimens. Meanwhile, species whose populations remained relatively stable frequently carried the fungus.

At first glance, these findings might seem to contradict the idea that chytrid caused the disappearances. The researchers believe the explanation may lie in differences in how individual species respond to the disease.

Some frogs may have been naturally capable of tolerating the infection, allowing them to survive even when the fungus was present. More vulnerable species, on the other hand, may have died so quickly after becoming infected that few or no infected individuals were ever collected.

"It's important to keep in mind that not all species suffered catastrophic losses at Boracéia," Boyette said. "The species that didn't decline may have naturally tolerated the fungus, allowing them to become infected without suffering mass mortality. By contrast, the species that declined most dramatically may have been so susceptible that infected frogs died before Heyer could collect them."

Together, the results suggest that chytrid spread rapidly among frogs with little previous exposure to the disease, with potentially devastating consequences for species unable to withstand infection.

Decades-Old Collections Help Solve a Wildlife Cold Case

For Michael Campana, a genomicist at NZCBI who contributed to the research, the findings demonstrate the extraordinary scientific value of natural history museums.

Specimens preserved many decades ago can contain biological evidence that researchers at the time had no way of recognizing. Modern testing methods now make it possible to revisit these collections and investigate outbreaks that occurred long before the responsible pathogens were discovered.

"Museum collectors could not have anticipated how important their collections would be to our modern conservation challenges, but without them, we would never be able to detect pathogens that went unnoticed for decades and reconstruct disease outbreaks that would otherwise remain a mystery," Campana said.

Understanding these past outbreaks could also help scientists anticipate future threats.

One growing concern involves another fungal pathogen, B. salamandrivorans, which is threatening salamander populations in Europe and could pose a serious danger to salamanders in North America.

By reconstructing how earlier fungal diseases emerged, spread, and affected different species, researchers hope to improve their ability to recognize and respond to similar threats before they cause widespread damage.

Brazil's Frogs Show Surprising Signs of Recovery

Despite the devastating losses recorded decades ago, the latest findings also offer encouraging evidence of recovery.

Working with researchers from the University of São Paulo, the team made six visits to Boracéia between 2022 and 2024 to investigate the amphibians living there today.

Of the 17 species represented in Heyer's historical museum collection, researchers located 12 during their modern surveys. The remaining five were not found, leaving their current status uncertain and raising concerns that some may have disappeared from the site entirely.

Nevertheless, the surveys indicate that most amphibian species at Boracéia have recovered since the severe declines of the early 1980s.

The fungus has not disappeared. Chytrid infections are still present among local frogs, but the pattern of infection suggests that species once heavily affected by the disease may have developed greater tolerance over successive generations.

That increased tolerance could help explain why many populations have survived and rebounded despite continuing exposure to the pathogen.

The findings highlight an important distinction between infection and mortality. A species can carry a dangerous pathogen without necessarily suffering catastrophic losses, particularly if its members can tolerate the infection.

What the Discovery Means for Future Amphibian Survival

Although the evidence strongly implicates chytrid in the historic declines at Boracéia, the researchers caution that their findings apply to this particular location. The results cannot automatically explain amphibian disappearances elsewhere in the Atlantic Forest.

Still, the study provides a compelling explanation for a longstanding local mystery and demonstrates how scientists can use historical specimens to reconstruct outbreaks that would otherwise remain poorly understood.

The investigation is also continuing.

Researchers are now examining DNA recovered from museum specimens to identify the genetic mechanisms that influenced how amphibians responded to chytrid infections in the past. These analyses could help reveal why some species were devastated while others survived.

Separate projects are using ancient environmental DNA to help fill gaps in historical specimen records. This approach involves searching for genetic traces left behind by organisms in their surroundings, potentially providing evidence of species and pathogens that were never directly collected.

Together, these efforts could reveal a much clearer history of how chytrid emerged, spread, and affected amphibian biodiversity over the past century.

By uncovering the biological changes that helped some frogs survive and recover, scientists may also gain valuable insights into protecting vulnerable species from future fungal epidemics.

It highlights the recovery of many frog populations due to increased tolerance, which has broad implications for biodiversity conservation and future disease management. The story is well-detailed, focused, and offers hope for protecting vulnerable species, fulfilling criteria for inspiring good news with meaningful environmental impact.
articles.personality_title: Scientists solve 50-year mystery of disappearing frogs in Brazil
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For nearly 50 years, scientists wondered why frogs vanished from Brazil's Atlantic Forest, a place rich in amphibian species. Starting in the 1970s, many frog populations suddenly dropped, but no one knew the real cause.

**What happened** – Researchers from the Smithsonian's National Zoo and Pennsylvania State University studied preserved frogs collected before and after the declines. They found that a deadly fungus called chytrid appeared in the area at the same time frogs disappeared. This fungus infects frogs and can kill them quickly. Some frog species died out, while others survived because they could tolerate the fungus.

**Impact** – This discovery explains a long-standing mystery about frog declines in this region. It also shows how some frogs have developed tolerance to the disease, helping their populations recover. Using old museum specimens helped scientists track the disease's arrival and spread decades ago, showing how valuable preserved animals are for understanding wildlife health.

**What's next step** – Scientists will study the DNA of these frogs to learn why some survived and others did not. They will also search for more evidence of past outbreaks using environmental DNA. This work could guide efforts to protect frogs and other amphibians from future fungal diseases worldwide.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After decades of mystery, scientists found that a deadly fungus caused frog disappearances in Brazil, but many frogs are now bouncing back thanks to natural tolerance.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les scientifiques résolvent le mystère de 50 ans sur la disparition des grenouilles au Brésil
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Pendant près de 50 ans, les scientifiques se sont demandé pourquoi les grenouilles disparaissaient de la forêt atlantique du Brésil, une région riche en espèces d’amphibiens. À partir des années 1970, de nombreuses populations de grenouilles ont chuté soudainement, sans que la cause soit connue.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs du Zoo national Smithsonian et de l’Université d’État de Pennsylvanie ont étudié des grenouilles conservées avant et après ces déclins. Ils ont découvert qu’un champignon mortel appelé chytride est apparu à la même époque que la disparition des grenouilles. Ce champignon infecte et tue rapidement les grenouilles. Certaines espèces ont disparu, tandis que d’autres ont survécu grâce à une tolérance naturelle.

**Impact** – Cette découverte explique un mystère ancien sur la baisse des grenouilles dans cette région. Elle montre aussi que certaines grenouilles ont développé une tolérance à la maladie, ce qui a aidé leur population à se rétablir. L’utilisation d’animaux conservés en musée a permis de suivre l’arrivée et la propagation de la maladie il y a des décennies, montrant l’importance de ces collections pour comprendre la santé de la faune.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques étudieront l’ADN de ces grenouilles pour comprendre pourquoi certaines ont survécu et d’autres non. Ils rechercheront aussi des preuves d’anciennes épidémies grâce à l’ADN environnemental. Ces travaux pourraient aider à protéger les grenouilles et autres amphibiens contre de futures maladies fongiques dans le monde.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Après des décennies de mystère, les scientifiques ont découvert qu’un champignon mortel a causé la disparition des grenouilles au Brésil, mais beaucoup reprennent vie grâce à une tolérance naturelle.
articles.personality_title_es: Científicos resuelven misterio de 50 años sobre desaparición de ranas en Brasil
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante casi 50 años, los científicos se preguntaron por qué las ranas desaparecían del Bosque Atlántico de Brasil, una zona rica en especies de anfibios. Desde los años 70, muchas poblaciones de ranas bajaron de forma repentina, pero no se conocía la causa.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores del Zoológico Nacional Smithsonian y la Universidad Estatal de Pensilvania estudiaron ranas conservadas antes y después de las caídas. Descubrieron que un hongo mortal llamado quítrido apareció justo cuando las ranas desaparecían. Este hongo infecta y mata rápidamente a las ranas. Algunas especies murieron, pero otras sobrevivieron porque podían tolerar la infección.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo explica un misterio antiguo sobre la disminución de ranas en esa región. También muestra que algunas ranas desarrollaron tolerancia a la enfermedad, ayudando a que sus poblaciones se recuperen. El uso de animales conservados en museos permitió a los científicos seguir la llegada y propagación del hongo hace décadas, mostrando lo valiosas que son estas colecciones para entender la salud animal.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos analizarán el ADN de estas ranas para entender por qué algunas sobrevivieron y otras no. También buscarán más pruebas de brotes antiguos usando ADN ambiental. Este trabajo podría ayudar a proteger a las ranas y otros anfibios de futuras enfermedades fúngicas en todo el mundo.

**Frase clave** – Tras décadas de misterio, los científicos descubrieron que un hongo mortal causó la desaparición de ranas en Brasil, pero muchas están regresando gracias a la tolerancia natural.

articles.title: What a historic ‘blue wave’ midterm means for climate action
articles.content:
The Democratic Party appeared set to win a commanding victory in Tuesday’s midterm elections. As of 11 p.m. Eastern on Tuesday night, the party was on track to gain control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, as well as several state governments. The party’s strong performance, driven in part by voters’ anger over inflation and the war in Iran, reached into traditional Republican strongholds like Ohio and South Carolina. A sweep would have profound consequences for climate action in the United States, even with President Donald Trump still in the White House.

Flipping control of Congress would allow the Democrats to hinder Trump’s numerous attempts to roll back federal climate policy. In the first two years of Trump’s term, party leaders could do little more than write strongly worded statements to administration officials. They were powerless to stop the suspension of clean energy funding, the elimination of climate rules for power plants and motor vehicles, and the hollowing-out of agencies like the U.S. Forest Service and the Federal Emergency Management Agency.

If Tuesday’s results hold, the party will have a lot more leverage. Democratic senators and members of Congress can issue subpoenas to force administration officials to testify before Congress, and could impeach Trump administration figures over funding clawbacks and staff reductions that Democrats have called unlawful. Democrats would also have control over must-pass funding bills, and Trump would have to negotiate with them in order to avoid a government shutdown. This could even lead to the restoration of some funding for energy and climate resilience programs that Republicans have been trying to whittle down.

Turnover at the state level, where officials are still counting votes, may be even more significant. Democrats could gain control of the state government in purple states, ending in some cases decades of Republican or divided government. This could allow them to pass meaningful climate policy for the first time — in Pennsylvania, for instance, state house Democrats have said they intend to pass bills making it easier to build community solar, warehouse solar, and battery energy storage, as well as preventing local governments from banning renewables. In Georgia, Democrats flipped both the governor’s mansion and control of the public service commission, which regulates electric utilities.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

While Trump’s approval ratings are underwater on almost every major issue, energy prices were among the most salient issues in many races. The gasoline price hike caused by Trump’s invasion of Iran was perhaps the most consequential, but voters in many places were also concerned about their heating bills (Maine) and homeowner’s insurance premiums (Florida). In places like Texas and Ohio, skepticism over the AI boom may also have driven voters to oust incumbents who supported data centers.

Here are some of the most consequential outcomes for climate change and the environment. We’ll continue to update this post as more results and analysis come in.

Supporters watch election results during a midterm election night watch party for Texas Democratic Senate candidate, State Rep. James Talarico at the Long Center on November 3, 2026 in Austin, Texas.

Brandon Bell / Getty Images

Texas elects Democratic senator for the first time in nearly 40 years

Texas joined other Southern states in flipping blue for the first time in decades. Senator-elect James Talarico, a Democrat, supports an all-of-the-above energy strategy, which includes protecting oil and gas jobs while also growing renewable energy. This moderate approach proved important in a state that provides over 40 percent of the nation’s oil and gas.

As a state representative, Talarico authored and introduced the Texas Climate Action Act in 2021. While the bill did not advance, it aimed to establish targets for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and set energy efficiency standards, with an emphasis on local resiliency.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Talarico beat out Republican Ken Paxton, the state’s attorney general, who is widely considered friendly to the oil and gas industry. He’s been embroiled in scandal for years and was impeached in 2023 by the Texas House. Paxton’s track record likely helped Democrats obtain this victory.

— Celeste Guajardo

Representative Kathy Castor holds a hearing for a committee in the House of Representatives. Castor, a leading Democrat climate hawk, survived a tough re-election challenge in a district drawn to eliminate her. Bill Clark / CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images

A climate hawk survives Republican redlining

Her district was redrawn to eliminate her, but voters in Florida’s 14th congressional district reelected Democratic Representative Kathy Castor anyway.



Castor — referred to as a “climate hawk” by E&E News — has spent much of her long career in Congress raising the alarm about climate change. Between 2019 and 2022 she chaired the House Select Committee on the Climate Crisis, and has otherwise made reducing carbon pollution and preparing communities for climate impacts central to her legislative agenda. In March, she backed the Energy Bills Relief Act, which proposed restoring energy upgrade tax credits and connecting more clean energy to the grid. She has also strongly opposed data centers in the Tampa area that she serves, warning that the facilities could drive up her constituents’ utility costs while straining local water supplies.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Democrats flip control of Georgia utility commission for first time in decades

Democrats secured both Public Service Commission seats on the Georgia ballot, giving the party majority control of the powerful utility regulation board for the first time in 30 years.

Democrat Peter Hubbard successfully defended his District 3 seat against a challenge from former commissioner Fitz Johnson, while Democrat Shelia Edwards defeated Republican Josh Tolbert to take the District 5 seat.

The commission regulates utilities, including the behemoth Georgia Power, meaning commissioners have final say over how the state’s largest utility makes energy and how much customers pay for it. The board has drawn increased scrutiny in recent years because of a series of rate hikes and the scramble to produce enough energy for the massive spike in demand that Georgia Power predicts will result from the data center boom. The utility’s plans to meet that demand rely heavily on fossil fuels.

Georgia is one of 10 states where utility regulators are elected rather than appointed.

— Emily Jones

A flip in an area devastated by Helene

In western North Carolina, where Hurricane Helene caused billions of dollars of damage two years ago, Democrat Jamie Ager defeated Republican Jennifer Balkcom for an open seat in the House of Representatives. Ager, a longtime farmer, made the area’s slow hurricane recovery a centerpiece of his campaign. He criticized Representative Chuck Edwards, who dropped out of the race after a sexual harassment scandal, for doing too little to deliver aid for Asheville and its surrounding counties. Grist reported last month that at least some voters blamed Republicans for the slow recovery. In a rally held on the eve of the election, President Trump promised to deliver more hurricane aid money, but only if North Carolina elected Republicans. The district around Asheville did not take the bait — not only did Ager win the state’s 11th House district, but Democrat Roy Cooper, the state’s former governor, easily won a Senate race, flipping a seat that had been held by Republicans.

— Jake Bittle

North Carolina Democratic congressional candidate Jamie Ager greets a supporter at a “Trunk or Treat” Halloween campaign event. Ager prevailed in a race for a seat in an area devastated by Hurricane Helene. Allison Joyce / Getty Images

Democrats win after attacking Republicans on data centers

At least three legislative seats flipped blue after Democrats aggressively criticized Republican incumbents for being too friendly to data centers. Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Senator Jon Husted in Ohio’s special Senate election after state Democrats put up billboards stating: “See that data center? Jon Husted did that.” Likewise, Democrat Paige Cognetti beat Republican Representative Rob Bresnahan in Pennsylvania’s 8th congressional district after she ran television ads associating Bresnahan with data centers and comparing tech companies to polluting mining corporations. Bresnahan has been revealed to have owned stock in data center companies. And in South Carolina’s Senate race, voters pushed Annie Andrews to a surprise win over Senator Darline Graham after she highlighted that a new pro-data center super PAC spent $1.5 million dollars on ads for her opponent, whom she nicknamed “Data Center Darline.”

Both Husted and Bresnahan had previously welcomed data centers to their regions, but later attempted unsuccessfully to pass regulations constraining them once the facilities became a hot-button issue. Data centers are massively unpopular with voters across the political spectrum, polls have shown. The facilities have become a growing source of demand for electricity from fossil fuels.

— Austin Corona and Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

A FEMA defender sails to victory in Florida

Representative Jared Moskowitz, a Democrat, easily hung onto his seat in Congress, surviving a challenge from Scott Singer, a Trump-backed Republican, in Florida’s redrawn 25th congressional district. His third-term victory defies the right-wing effort to make his district significantly redder with new boundaries, and keeps one of America’s most vocal FEMA reformers in Congress.

Moskowitz, once appointed Florida’s emergency management director by Governor Ron DeSantis, championed bipartisan legislation to pull FEMA out of the Department of Homeland Security and make it an independent, cabinet-level agency — just as the Trump administration seeks to cut its funding and shift more responsibility onto states. He has also introduced bills that would let states voluntarily administer federal disaster housing and public assistance, and proposed a reinsurance backstop that would help cover catastrophic losses after disasters like hurricanes.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

Detroit, Michigan – Climate protesters demonstrate against DTE Energy’s request to hike electricity rates to pay for more fossil fuel plants. Voters in Michigan passed an amendment that would restrict uitilities’ political campaign contributions. Jim West/ UCG / Universal Images Group via Getty Images

Michigan gets utility money out of politics

Voters in Michigan passed a measure to limit corporate spending in elections, and in a nationwide first, successfully went after the state’s electric and gas utilities. Supporters of Proposal 2 leveraged ratepayers’ growing dissatisfaction with utilities around power bills, unreliable service, and data centers. The measure is one of the most ambitious attempts in the country to limit corporate influence in politics, which it will do by preventing utility-funded political action groups and utility executives from contributing to state political campaigns. Groups that oppose the measure have contended that Prop 2 will stifle corporations’ speech protections under the 2010 Citizens United case. And while experts are fairly confident the measure will face legal challenges and won’t get all utility money out of politics, Prop 2 advocates maintain it’s a step toward accountability.

— Vivian La

A governor who at least acknowledges climate change in Florida

Republican Byron Donalds has defeated Democrat David Jolly for occupancy of Florida’s governor’s mansion. Donalds, who currently represents Florida’s 19th congressional district, will be the state’s first Black governor. He doesn’t believe humans play any role in global warming, but he’s more willing to discuss the issue than the current governor, Ron DeSantis, who signed the state’s infamous “don’t say climate change” law.

That matters in a state especially battered by sea level rise, coastal erosion, and storms. The skyrocketing costs of home insurance were a central issue in this race, and Donalds promised to bring them down by increasing competition in the state’s private market. In 2025, Donalds notably co-introduced bipartisan legislation with Democrat Jared Moskowitz to reform federal disaster aid by making FEMA an independent cabinet-level agency. In the weeks before voters went to the polls, he also pledged investment in restoring coastal habitats. Donalds seems likely to carry on DeSantis’ other environmental policies, such as supporting data center development and attacking wind and solar projects.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

A campaign sign for Florida Republican Senate candidate, Ashley Moody outside a polling station on November 3, 2026 in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida. Saul Martinez / Getty Images

A MAGA loyalist who says no to drilling in Florida

Republican Senator Ashley Moody defeated the progressive Democrat Angie Nixon to retain her seat, which Governor DeSantis appointed her to last year. Moody’s brief stint in Washington hints at what’s to come: She introduced a resolution to overturn Biden-era efficiency standards and supported the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which ended federal tax credits for clean energy installations, like rooftop solar and batteries. Previously, as Florida’s attorney general, she joined a lawsuit challenging emissions reduction targets on highways.

But in Florida, a state grappling with coastal erosion and rising sea levels, some environmental protections are popular across party lines: Last year, even as Trump pushed to open offshore drilling in other states, Moody introduced the American Shores Protection Act to ban the practice off Florida’s coast through 2032.

— Sachi Kitajima Mulkey

articles.title: Stanford scientists discovered bleached coral can heal through touch
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Two coral fragments fell over in a Stanford lab tank. When they touched, one healed the other. The bleached fragment, starved of the symbiotic algae that give coral both its color and its nutrition, began recovering within days. “We watched the healthy coral send over these colourful beneficial algae […]
The post Stanford scientists discovered bleached coral can heal through touch first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Two coral fragments fell over in a Stanford lab tank. When they touched, one healed the other.

The bleached fragment, starved of the symbiotic algae that give coral both its color and its nutrition, began recovering within days. “We watched the healthy coral send over these colourful beneficial algae over to the bleached corals, and we watched its colour restore basically in front of our eyes,” said ocean scientist Danny Collins. Within a couple of weeks, the dying coral had recovered to the point where it was indistinguishable from its healthy neighbor. “We were blown away,” Collins said. “It does seem like this could open a door to possible reef restoration.”

The findings, published last month in Science Advances, suggest that bleached coral is not necessarily dead, and that it can recover faster than researchers expected.

The magic of the tissue bridge

The recovery requires direct physical contact and a genetic match. When Collins’s team separated the fragments by a few millimeters, nothing happened. When they introduced corals from different genetic backgrounds, the corals rejected each other the way a body might reject a donated organ.

When genetic clones made contact, their tissues fused. “They create a tissue bridge that kind of acts as a nutrient highway that allows for the healthy coral to then send over nutrients and this colourful algae over to the bleached coral,” Collins said.

Coral is a colonial animal, a single organism made of thousands to millions of individual polyps. Fragments of the same genetic background recognize each other on contact and merge rather than fight. Collins noted this serves a natural function. If a piece breaks off in a wave, it can reconnect with the original colony.

96 percent of reefs are at risk

The International Union for Conservation of Nature announced that about 96 percent of the world’s shallow-water reef systems are critically endangered and could disappear by 2075. Coral reefs support between a quarter and a third of all marine species, along with fisheries and coastal economies that hundreds of millions of people depend on.

Coral scientist Julia Cole, who was not involved in the study, called the Stanford findings “a glimmer of light.” Cole chairs the Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences at the University of Michigan. She was enthusiastic but clear-eyed about scale. “If you think about the scale of reefs as kilometers, or in the case of the biggest reefs, thousands of kilometers … something that requires coral-to-coral contact, it would be a very meticulous and kind of overwhelming project,” she said.

Collins’s team is working on extracting algae from healthy reefs, culturing it in labs, and deploying it to protect at-risk reefs ahead of expected bleaching events. “We hope in the near future we can have some interventions that actually could be field deployable and possibly scalable,” he said.

The restoration work doesn’t address what’s warming the ocean in the first place. “We know how to solve the warming climate that’s causing these problems,” Cole said. “It comes back to getting serious about reducing greenhouse gas emissions, getting off of fossil fuels and transitioning to a clean-energy economy.”

Source study: Science Advances – Rapid coral bleaching recovery via symbiont transfer from healthy corals

articles.personality_title: Stanford scientists find bleached coral can heal by touching healthy coral
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Coral reefs are vital underwater ecosystems that support many sea creatures and help people who rely on fishing and coastal jobs. But about 96 percent of the world’s coral reefs are in danger because of warming oceans, which cause coral bleaching. Bleached coral loses the tiny algae that give it color and food, making it weak and often leading to death.

**What happened** – Scientists at Stanford University discovered that when a bleached coral piece physically touches a healthy coral piece of the same genetic type, it can start healing. In their lab, two coral fragments accidentally fell and touched. The healthy coral sent algae to the bleached one, which began to regain its color and strength in just days. After a couple of weeks, the bleached coral looked as healthy as the other.

**Impact** – This discovery is important because it shows bleached coral is not always dead and can recover faster than we thought. The healing only happens when corals are genetically matched and physically connected, creating a “tissue bridge” that lets nutrients and algae move between them. This natural process could help scientists develop new ways to restore coral reefs, which are shrinking worldwide.

**What's next step** – The researchers are now working on growing healthy algae in labs and sending them to endangered reefs before bleaching happens. They hope to create treatments that can be used in the ocean to protect corals on a larger scale. However, experts say this won’t fix the root problem of ocean warming, which needs global efforts to reduce greenhouse gases and switch to clean energy.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Stanford scientists found that bleached coral can recover by touching healthy coral of the same kind, offering a new way to help save endangered reefs.

articles.personality_title_es: Científicos de Stanford descubren que el coral blanqueado puede sanar al tocar coral sano
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los arrecifes de coral son ecosistemas marinos importantes que sostienen muchas especies y ayudan a personas que dependen de la pesca y actividades costeras. Pero aproximadamente el 96 % de los arrecifes están en peligro por el calentamiento de los océanos, que causa el blanqueo del coral. El coral blanqueado pierde las algas que le dan color y alimento, debilitándolo y a menudo provocando su muerte.

**Qué pasó** – Científicos de la Universidad de Stanford descubrieron que cuando un fragmento de coral blanqueado toca físicamente un coral sano del mismo tipo genético, puede empezar a sanar. En su laboratorio, dos fragmentos de coral se cayeron y se tocaron por accidente. El coral sano envió algas al coral blanqueado, que comenzó a recuperar su color y fuerza en pocos días. Después de un par de semanas, el coral blanqueado se veía tan sano como el otro.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo es importante porque demuestra que el coral blanqueado no siempre está muerto y puede recuperarse más rápido de lo que se pensaba. La sanación solo ocurre cuando los corales están genéticamente iguales y conectados físicamente, formando un “puente de tejido” que permite que nutrientes y algas pasen entre ellos. Este proceso natural podría ayudar a desarrollar nuevas formas de restaurar los arrecifes, que están disminuyendo en todo el mundo.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores están trabajando en cultivar algas saludables en laboratorios y llevarlas a arrecifes en peligro antes de que ocurra el blanqueo. Esperan crear tratamientos que puedan usarse en el océano para proteger corales a mayor escala. Sin embargo, los expertos dicen que esto no soluciona el problema principal del calentamiento oceánico, que necesita esfuerzos globales para reducir gases de efecto invernadero y usar energía limpia.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Científicos de Stanford encontraron que el coral blanqueado puede recuperarse al tocar coral sano del mismo tipo, ofreciendo una nueva forma de ayudar a salvar arrecifes en peligro.
